objectives: Use the price-floor model to predict how a minimum wage above the equilibrium wage affects wages, employment, and the surplus of labor in a competitive labor market.
Explain why real-world evidence on minimum wages is mixed and still debated, including factors economists point to, such as how high the minimum is relative to local wages and employer market power.
Compare labor policies such as the minimum wage, job training, job-search help, and earned-income support by their benefits, costs, and trade-offs.

concepts.term: Minimum wage as a price floor
concepts.definition: A legal lower limit on the wage employers may pay. In a competitive labor market, it works like a price floor: it matters (is binding) only if it is set above the equilibrium wage. Under monopsony (see below), a floor below the competitive wage can still matter if it is above the wage the employer pays.

When the wage is held above equilibrium, the quantity of labor supplied is greater than the quantity of labor demanded. In the simple competitive model, the gap is a surplus of labor: people who want jobs at that wage but are not hired.

Studies of real minimum wage increases reach different conclusions: some find reduced hiring of low-skill workers, while others find little or no effect on employment. Economists continue to debate the methods and results. To explain the differences, they point to factors such as how high the minimum is compared with local wages and how much power employers have to set wages.

A monopsony is a labor market with a single employer (or a few dominant ones) that can set wages. Because workers have few alternatives, in the standard model such an employer hires fewer workers and pays a lower wage than a competitive labor market would.

Policies that help people return to work: training or retraining to fix skill mismatches (structural unemployment) and job-search help to speed up matching (frictional unemployment). They cost public money and their results depend on program design.

A payment, often delivered through the tax system, that adds to the income of low-wage workers and grows with earnings up to a limit, so it rewards work. In the U.S., the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) is an example. It is paid for by taxpayers rather than employers, and it shrinks as income rises above a certain level.

beginner.summary: A minimum wage is a lowest legal wage. In the simplest model, setting it above the market wage helps the workers who keep their jobs but leaves more people wanting work than employers want to hire. Real-world results are debated, and there are other ways to help low-wage workers.

sections.heading: A floor under wages
paragraphs: Many places have a law that says employers cannot pay less than a certain amount per hour. That amount is the minimum wage. In Course 2 you met the price floor, a legal lowest price. A minimum wage is a price floor for work. If the minimum is lower than the wage the market already pays, it changes nothing. It only matters when it is set above the market wage.

sections.heading: The simple model's prediction
paragraphs: Suppose the market wage for a job is $14 an hour and a law sets the minimum at $16. At the higher wage, more people want those jobs. But each worker now costs employers more, so in the simple model they hire fewer people. The result: more people want work than there are jobs. That gap is a surplus of labor, and it shows up as unemployment. Workers who keep their jobs earn more; some people who would have been hired at $14 are not hired.

sections.heading: What happens in real life is debated
paragraphs: Economists have studied many real minimum wage increases, and they do not all agree on what happened. Some studies find fewer jobs for low-skill workers; others find little change. A small increase in a place where wages are already high is different from a big jump in a place where wages are low.

Another reason is that some employers have the power to set wages. Imagine a town where one big company is almost the only place to work. Workers have few other choices, so the company can pay less than a competitive market would. In a simple model of a town like that, a minimum wage that is not set too high can raise pay without cutting jobs. Whether that describes a real town is a question for evidence, not just theory.

sections.heading: Other tools
paragraphs: A minimum wage is not the only option. Training programs teach new skills, so workers can move into jobs that pay more. Job-search help, like a job center, helps people find openings faster. Earned-income support adds money to low-wage workers' pay through the tax system, and the more they earn (up to a limit), the more support they get. Each tool costs something: training and support cost public money, and none of them works perfectly for everyone.

intermediate.summary: A binding minimum wage raises the wage of those employed, lowers the quantity of labor demanded, and raises the quantity supplied, creating a surplus of labor in the competitive model. To explain why real-world effects differ, economists point to factors such as how high the minimum is relative to local wages and how much power employers have to set wages. Other labor policies have their own trade-offs.

sections.heading: Binding and non-binding minimums
paragraphs: On a labor market graph with the wage on the vertical axis, the minimum wage is a horizontal line. If the line is below the equilibrium wage, the market wage is already higher and the law has no effect (non-binding). If the line is above the equilibrium wage, employers must pay at least that amount and the market cannot reach equilibrium (binding).

sections.heading: Reading the graph
paragraphs: At a binding minimum wage, read two quantities off the graph. The labor demand curve shows how many workers employers want to hire at that wage, which is less than equilibrium employment. The labor supply curve shows how many people want to work at that wage, which is more. In the competitive model, employment equals the quantity demanded, and the horizontal gap between the curves is the surplus of labor. The workers who are employed earn more than before, so the policy creates both winners and losers.

How big the effects are depends on the slopes. If employers can easily replace labor with machines or cut back output, labor demand is more responsive and the drop in employment is larger. If few extra people enter the market at the higher wage, labor supply is less responsive and the surplus is smaller.

sections.heading: Why the evidence is mixed
paragraphs: Researchers measure what actually happens after minimum wages rise, and their results differ. Reviews of earlier research found that most studies reported some reduction in low-skill employment after minimum wage increases, while a number of later studies find small or no measurable employment effects; economists continue to debate the methods and results on both sides. Economists also argue about how to weigh job losses for some workers against higher incomes for many others.

Economists point to factors that may help explain the range of results. First, the level: a minimum that is modest compared with typical local wages is likely to have smaller effects than one far above them. Second, market structure: where a few employers have the power to set wages (monopsony), they pay less and hire fewer workers than a competitive market would. In the standard monopsony model, a minimum wage set between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage can raise both pay and employment. How common such markets are, and how much they explain real results, is still debated.

sections.heading: Comparing labor policies
paragraphs: Training and retraining target structural unemployment by building the human capital employers want; the trade-off is cost and uncertain results. Job-search help targets frictional unemployment by speeding up matching; it is cheaper but does not create jobs or skills. Earned-income support raises the income of low-wage workers and encourages work because it grows with earnings; it is paid by taxpayers instead of employers, and as it phases out at higher incomes, each extra dollar earned adds less to take-home income. Unemployment insurance supports people while they search. It also lowers the cost of staying unemployed, so some people may search less intensely, and how long benefits last can matter for how quickly people return to work. How big this effect is depends on program design.

advanced.summary: With L_d = a − bW and L_s = c + dW, a binding minimum wage W_min > W* lowers employment by b(W_min − W*) and creates a surplus of labor of (b + d)(W_min − W*). Total wage income of employed workers can rise or fall. In the standard monopsony model, the competitive prediction can reverse over a range of minimum wages, which is one reason the evidence is contested.

sections.heading: The competitive model in equations
paragraphs: Let W* = (a − c)/(b + d). If W_min ≤ W*, the floor is non-binding. If W_min > W*, employment is L_d(W_min) = a − bW_min, so the employment loss is ΔL = b(W_min − W*), and the surplus of labor is L_s(W_min) − L_d(W_min) = (b + d)(W_min − W*). Part of the surplus is people who were already in the market and lost or did not get jobs (b(W_min − W*)); the rest is new job seekers drawn in by the higher wage (d(W_min − W*)).

Total wage income of those employed changes from W*·L* to W_min·L_d(W_min). Whether it rises depends on how responsive labor demand is: if a 1% rise in the wage lowers employment by less than 1% (inelastic labor demand), total wage income rises even though fewer people work.

sections.heading: Monopsony and contested evidence
paragraphs: A monopsonist faces the upward-sloping labor supply curve, so hiring one more worker means paying a higher wage to all workers. Its marginal cost of labor is above the wage, and it hires where labor demand equals that marginal cost. The result is employment L_m below the competitive level L_c and a wage W_m below the competitive wage W_c.

A floor at or below W_m does not bind. A minimum wage W_min with W_m < W_min ≤ W_c makes the marginal cost of labor equal to W_min over a range of employment, so the firm hires the number of workers on the labor supply curve at W_min, which is more than L_m. In this range of the standard monopsony model, a minimum wage raises both the wage and employment, and employment is highest when W_min = W_c (it reaches L_c). Above W_c, the firm hires only the quantity on labor demand, so employment falls as the floor rises. Employment drops below the original monopsony level L_m only when W_min is higher than the height of labor demand at L_m, which equals the monopsonist's marginal cost of labor at L_m. Because real labor markets differ in employer power and in how high the minimum is relative to local wages, empirical studies can reasonably reach different conclusions, and the debate is not settled.

sections.heading: Policy design and trade-offs
paragraphs: Earned-income support is typically designed with a phase-in rate (support rises with earnings), a flat range, and a phase-out rate (support falls as earnings rise further). During the phase-out, each extra dollar earned raises take-home income by only (1 − phase-out rate), which acts like an extra tax on work. A slower phase-out means a smaller extra tax on each dollar earned, but it costs more and stretches the phase-out range over more workers. Training and job-search programs should be judged by how much they raise employment and earnings compared with what would have happened without them, relative to their cost.

worked_examples.title: How many people want jobs that are not there?
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: A city sets a minimum wage of $17 per hour for its restaurant jobs, which is above the market wage. At $17, 260 people want restaurant jobs, but restaurants want to hire only 220 workers. In the simple model, how large is the surplus of labor?
steps: Quantity of labor supplied at $17 = 260 people.
Quantity of labor demanded at $17 = 220 workers.
worked_examples.answer: In the simple competitive model, 40 people want restaurant jobs at $17 but are not hired. The 220 people who are hired earn more than the market wage.

worked_examples.title: A binding minimum wage on the graph
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: In a market for entry-level retail workers, labor demand is L_d = 800 − 20W and labor supply is L_s = 50 + 30W. Find the equilibrium. Then a minimum wage of $18 per hour is introduced. Find employment and the surplus of labor at the minimum wage.
steps: $18 is above $15, so the minimum wage is binding.
Employment falls from 500 to 440 (by 60), and the surplus of labor is 590 − 440 = 150.
worked_examples.answer: Without the minimum wage, W* = $15 and 500 workers are employed. At $18, employers hire 440 workers while 590 want jobs, so the simple model predicts 60 fewer jobs and a surplus of 150 workers.

worked_examples.title: Winners, losers, and total wage income
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example (the market from worked example 2): Using the formulas, confirm the employment loss and the surplus of labor at W_min = $18. Then compare the total hourly wage income of employed workers before and after the minimum wage.
steps: Employment loss = b(W_min − W*) = 20 × (18 − 15) = 60. Surplus = (b + d)(W_min − W*) = 50 × 3 = 150. Both match worked example 2.
The wage rose by 20% (3/15) while employment fell by 12% (60/500), so labor demand is inelastic in this range and total wage income rises.
worked_examples.answer: Total wage income of employed workers rises from $7,500 to $7,920 per hour, but 60 fewer people are employed. The policy raises the group's income while some individuals lose work, which is exactly the trade-off economists debate.

worked_examples.title: Earned-income support during the phase-in
worked_examples.problem: Hypothetical example: An earned-income support program adds 20 cents for every dollar a low-wage worker earns, up to a limit. A worker earns $6,000 in a year, which is below the limit. How much support does the worker receive, and what is the worker's total income?
steps: Each extra dollar earned in this range brings $1.20 of income, so the program rewards working more.
worked_examples.answer: The worker receives $1,200 of support, for a total income of $7,200. The support is paid by taxpayers, not by the employer, which is one difference from a minimum wage.

graphs.title: A minimum wage above the equilibrium wage
graphs.caption: Hypothetical example (worked examples 2 and 3). Without a minimum wage, labor demand and labor supply meet at W = $15 and L = 500. At the $18 minimum wage, employers hire 440 workers while 590 want to work: a surplus of labor of 150 in the simple competitive model.

real_world_examples.title: Minimum wage and living wage debates
paragraphs: Supporters of higher minimum wages and local living wage laws argue that full-time workers should earn enough to stay out of poverty. Critics warn that higher wage floors can reduce hiring of low-skill workers. Studies point in different directions, and weighing job losses for some against income gains for others has no simple answer.

real_world_examples.title: One employer, few alternatives
paragraphs: The classic example of monopsony is a town with a single large employer, such as a mining company, where workers have nowhere else nearby to work. Such an employer can pay less and hire fewer workers than a competitive labor market would. Laws such as minimum wages are among the tools that aim to balance the bargaining power of workers and employers.

real_world_examples.title: Rewarding work through the tax system
paragraphs: The U.S. Earned Income Tax Credit gives low-income working families a credit that rises with earnings, levels off, and then gradually shrinks as income rises further. Because it grows with earnings, it is widely seen as rewarding work. Other support programs that shrink quickly as earnings rise can make extra work barely pay off.

sdg_case.title: Raising low-wage workers' living standards: which tool?
paragraphs: SDG target 8.5 aims for full and productive employment and decent work for all women and men, including young people and persons with disabilities, and equal pay for work of equal value. SDG target 8.8 calls for protecting labour rights and promoting safe and secure working environments for all workers.

Hypothetical situation: A region's leaders want to raise the living standards of workers in low-paid jobs such as cleaning, food service, and warehouse work. Some local employers are large and face little competition for workers; others are small shops with thin profit margins. The leaders are comparing three approaches.

options.name: Raise the regional minimum wage by a moderate amount
benefits: Workers who keep their jobs earn more immediately, and the cost does not come from the public budget.
Where large employers hold wages down, a moderate floor may raise pay without cutting jobs.
costs: Small shops may hire fewer people, cut hours, or raise prices.
If the floor is high compared with local wages, some low-skill workers may find it harder to get hired.
assumptions: The increase is modest relative to local wages, and employers' wage-setting power is significant.

options.name: Expand earned-income support paid through taxes
benefits: Raises low-wage workers' income without raising employers' labor costs, so hiring is less likely to fall.
Rewards work because support grows with earnings.
costs: Costs public money, which requires higher taxes or cuts elsewhere.
As support phases out, extra earnings add less to take-home pay, weakening the incentive to work more hours.
assumptions: The region can fund the program, and eligible workers actually claim it.

options.name: Fund skills training and stronger enforcement of labor rights and safety rules
benefits: Training raises productivity, which can lift wages over the long run.
Enforcement protects workers' rights and safety now, directly supporting SDG target 8.8.
costs: Results take time, and training does not help everyone equally.
Inspections and programs cost money and need trained staff.
assumptions: Training matches local job needs, and inspectors have the resources to act.

discussion: Who pays and who benefits under each option? Using the labor market graph and the idea of employer market power, explain under what conditions you would choose a minimum wage increase, and when you would prefer another tool or a combination.

key_takeaways: A minimum wage is a price floor for labor. In the simple competitive model, a binding minimum raises the wage of those employed, lowers employment, and creates a surplus of labor.
Real-world evidence is mixed and debated. To explain why results differ, economists point to factors such as how high the minimum is relative to local wages and employer market power (monopsony).
Training, job-search help, and earned-income support target different problems and have their own costs; good labor policy weighs these trade-offs rather than relying on a single tool.
